hero.title: Electromagnetic Broadcasting
hero.lead: Electromagnetic waves travel through the vacuum at the speed of light without needing a material medium, and radio waves among them are used for audio and video broadcasting by two methods: the ground wave and the sky wave.

objectives: Describes the properties of electromagnetic waves and how they are generated.
Lists the bands of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of wavelength.
Distinguishes between the ground wave and the sky wave, and the conditions for achieving communication with each.
Explains the role of the ionosphere and the geostationary orbit in broadcasting radio and television waves.

content.heading: 💡 5-5 Electromagnetic Broadcasting
content.html: It is well known that electromagnetic waves do not necessarily need a material medium to travel through, and that they are transverse waves; they are generated by the oscillation of free electrons in a conductor, since the origin of these waves is oscillating electric charges. This oscillation produces two time-varying, coupled, mutually perpendicular electric and magnetic fields along the direction of propagation, and these waves travel through the vacuum at the speed of light.

content.label: 📌 Definition — The Electromagnetic Spectrum
content.html: The electromagnetic spectrum consists of bands of different wavelengths, the most important of which are: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet rays, visible light, infrared rays, microwaves, and radio waves.

content.label: 🔍 Explanation — The Relationship Between Wavelength and Oscillation Rate
content.html: Radio waves are generally used in audio and video broadcasting, and the technical use of electromagnetic waves depends on how easily the different wavelengths can be identified and produced. Wavelength is related to the oscillation rate of the electrons at the source of the wave energy: the longer the wavelength, the slower the oscillation, and so on.

content.heading: 5-5-1 The Ground Wave and the Sky Wave
content.html: The Earth is approximately spherical, with a diameter and radius of about (6400 km), and a circumference of its largest circle of about (40000 km). The bulge between two points and the distance between them of about (250 km) exceeds (1 km). This bulge represents a significant obstacle preventing waves from propagating between the two points; nevertheless, communication between points separated by the curvature or irregularity of the Earth's surface can be achieved if one of the following conditions is met:

content.label: 🔢 List — Conditions for Achieving Radio Communication Despite the Curvature of the Earth's Surface
content.html:
1. The waves travel along paths that follow the curvature and bulges of the Earth's surface.
  2. Mounting both the transmitting antenna and the receiving antenna at suitable heights provides a direct line of sight between the two antennas.
  3. Providing intermediate broadcasting stations between the transmitting station and the receiving station, positioned at the bulges of the Earth's surface whose height is comparable to the wavelength of the propagating wave, for radio waves traveling close to the Earth's surface.
Radio waves are broadcast by two methods:

content.label: 📌 Definition — The First Method: Ground Waves
content.html: This kind of wave is called a ground wave, and it travels directly along the Earth's surface (close to it); however, because it propagates in straight lines, it is unable to maintain communications except over relatively short distances, owing to the curvature of the Earth.

content.label: 📌 Definition — The Second Method: Sky Waves
content.html: This is achieved by means of indirect waves called sky waves, which can maintain communications between two distant locations not lying on a direct line. This type of communication depends primarily on the presence of the ionosphere in the atmosphere, which reflects the indirect waves back down to the Earth.

ruleBoxes.html: The ground wave travels close to the Earth's surface in near-straight lines, so it reaches only relatively short distances because of the Earth's curvature.

labels.captionGround: The ground wave travels close to the Earth's surface in near-straight lines, so it reaches only relatively short distances because of the Earth's curvature.
labels.captionSky: The sky wave rises toward the ionosphere and reflects off it back to the Earth, maintaining communication between two distant points not lying on a direct line.

content.heading: 🌙 Day-Night Differences in Wave Propagation and Satellite Communications
content.html:
During the night, because sunlight is absent, the lower layer of the ionosphere, called the D-layer, which is responsible for attenuating radio waves during the day, disappears.

The microwaves used continuously for television transmission are able to penetrate the ionosphere, and only a small amount of them is reflected back, which limits television broadcasting to short distances only. This has been overcome by using artificial satellites placed in fixed orbits around the Earth.

content.label: 📌 Definition — The Geostationary Orbit
content.html: The geostationary orbit is an orbit in which a satellite revolves at the same rate as the Earth's rotation and lies in the plane of the equator, allowing it to stay in a fixed position relative to the Earth. Any satellite in a geostationary orbit can pick up a fixed signal from a fixed station within its range and retransmit it to a new station located within the satellite's geographic footprint.

questions.question: Electromagnetic waves travel through the vacuum:
options: Only with the help of a material medium
At the speed of light, without needing a material medium
They do not travel through the vacuum at all
questions.explain: Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves that need no material medium, and they travel through the vacuum at the speed of light.

questions.question: The shortest wavelengths in the electromagnetic spectrum belong to:
questions.explain: The electromagnetic spectrum begins (from shortest to longest wavelength) with gamma rays, then X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, and finally radio waves.

questions.question: The wave that relies on reflecting off the ionosphere to reach distant places not lying on a direct line is called:
questions.explain: The sky wave reflects off the ionosphere to maintain communication between two distant locations not lying on a direct line.

questions.question: The geostationary orbit is the orbit in which a satellite revolves:
options: At the same rate as the Earth's rotation, so it stays in a fixed position relative to it
In the direction opposite to the Earth's rotation
Around one of the poles only
questions.explain: The geostationary orbit lies in the plane of the equator, and a satellite in it revolves at the same rate as the Earth's rotation, staying fixed relative to a location on the Earth's surface.

summary.heading: 📋 Lesson Summary
items: Electromagnetic waves: transverse waves arising from the oscillation of electric charges, needing no material medium, and traveling at the speed of light.
The electromagnetic spectrum (from shortest to longest wavelength): gamma, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio.
The ground wave: travels close to the Earth's surface in straight lines, covering relatively short distances because of the Earth's curvature.
The sky wave: reflects off the ionosphere to cover long distances not lying on a direct line.
The D-layer disappears at night, reducing wave attenuation; microwaves penetrate the ionosphere, requiring geostationary satellites to rebroadcast them.
